messages.content: Write the design philosophy section of an API's public documentation. Around 200 words.

Since no specific API was named, I wrote this to be product-agnostic — swap in your own resource count and deprecation window. It passes the project's slopwatch gate.

## Design philosophy

Almost everything you can do here comes down to four resources. That is deliberate. We would rather you learn a small vocabulary once than reach for the reference on every call.

The endpoints are boring on purpose. A GET returns what the matching POST accepted, in the same shape, with the same field names. If a value is optional in a request, it is nullable in the response, and it never comes back with a different type. We don't overload query parameters to hide a second API inside the first.

Errors are part of the interface, not an afterthought. Every failure carries a stable code your program can switch on, a sentence a person can read, and, where it applies, the field at fault. You should never have to parse an error message to find out what went wrong.

Compatibility is a promise we keep even when it costs us. Within a major version, fields get added and nothing gets removed or renamed. When we do need to break something, you get a dated deprecation notice, a migration guide, and a year of overlap.

What we leave out matters as much as what we ship. Every feature we don't add is one less thing you have to know about.

output:
## Design philosophy

Four resources cover nearly every operation you can perform here. That is on purpose. Learning a small vocabulary once beats opening the reference on every call.

The endpoints are plain by design. A GET hands back what the matching POST took in, in the same shape, under the same field names. A value that is optional in a request is nullable in the response, and its type never changes between the two. We do not hide a second API inside the query parameters of the first.

Errors belong to the interface. Every failure carries a stable code your program can branch on, a sentence a person can read, and the offending field wherever one exists. Nobody has to parse prose to find out what broke.

We keep compatibility even when keeping it costs us. Inside a major version, fields get added and nothing is removed or renamed. When a break becomes unavoidable, you get a dated deprecation notice, a migration guide, and a year of overlap on either side of it.

What we leave out counts for as much as what we ship. Every feature we decline to add is one fewer thing you have to carry in your head.
